section_1.title: Geometric Interpretation of Linear Systems
section_1.content: Introduce a system of linear equations as the intersection of geometric objects (lines in 2D, planes in 3D). Explain that solving Ax=b is equivalent to finding the intersection point of these geometric spaces.
section_1.example: Visualizing two equations: x + y = 2 and x - y = 0 as two intersecting lines on a 2D plane; the intersection (1, 1) is the solution.

section_2.title: Column Space: Where Can We Reach?
section_2.content: Shift perspective from equations to vectors. Define the column space as the set of all possible linear combinations of the column vectors of A. This is the 'reach' or 'span' of the matrix.
section_2.example: Imagine a robot arm with two segments (column vectors). The column space is the entire 2D plane the robot can reach, or just a single line if the segments are parallel.

section_3.title: Null Space: The 'Ghost' Vectors
section_3.content: Define the null space as the set of all vectors x such that Ax = 0. Geometrically, these are the directions that the matrix collapses onto the origin (the 'kernel').
section_3.example: Think of a camera lens flattening a 3D forest onto a 2D photo; the null space is the line of sight along which all objects appear at the same pixel point.

section_4.title: Inverse Matrices: The Reversal Process
section_4.content: Introduce the inverse matrix as the 'undo' operation. Geometrically, if A transforms space, A-inverse maps the resulting point back to its original coordinate. Emphasize that this only works if the matrix doesn't 'crush' space (i.e., it must be full rank).
section_4.example: A cat stretches a rubber sheet (Matrix A); the inverse (A^-1) is the operation that perfectly shrinks the sheet back to its original, unstretched state.

section_5.title: Synthesis and Summary
section_5.content: Connect the concepts: If a matrix is invertible, the column space is the full space, and the null space is only the zero vector. If it is not, space is collapsed, and the inverse cannot exist.
section_5.example: A 'magic mirror' analogy: If the mirror (Matrix) is flat, it preserves the image (invertible). If the mirror is bent/warped (singular), it loses information, and you cannot 'un-bend' the image back to reality.
